title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 16
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Land Set Aside
passages.text:
A. The public park is a recent institution presented as an ancient one. Open ground existed in cities before the nineteenth century — commons, churchyards, market squares — but these were working spaces with rights attached, used for grazing, drying cloth or holding fairs. Land set aside purely for the recreation of an urban population, maintained at public expense and open to anyone, is an invention of industrial cities and was contested when it appeared.

B. The arguments made for the first parks were not the arguments made today. Advocates spoke of public health in terms of air: crowded districts were held to generate disease through foul atmosphere, and open ground was proposed as a source of clean air to dilute it. The theory was wrong. The parks were nonetheless built, and their health benefits — through exercise, cooling and mental respite — turned out to be real for reasons nobody at the time advanced.

C. A second argument was explicitly about behaviour, and it reads uncomfortably now. Parks were promoted as places where the industrial working population could be observed taking rational recreation instead of drinking, and where the presence of respectable visitors would encourage restraint. Rules were extensive, keepers were employed to enforce them, and activities that the intended beneficiaries actually favoured — informal football, gambling, unlicensed selling — were frequently prohibited.

D. Funding shaped what was built more than design theory did. Where parks were financed by adjacent land sales, they were laid out to maximise the value of the plots around them: perimeter roads, ornamental frontages, and layouts that made surrounding houses desirable. Where they were financed by subscription or bequest, the constraints differed and so did the results. The distinctive form of the nineteenth-century park is legible as a financing arrangement before it is legible as an aesthetic.

E. Maintenance has always been the weak point and remains so. A park is cheap to create relative to its running cost, and the running cost is invisible when it is being met and obvious when it is not. Budgets for parks are politically easy to reduce because deterioration is gradual, reversible in appearance for a while, and produces no immediate constituency — and the resulting cycle of decline and periodic capital rescue is more expensive over decades than steady maintenance would have been.

F. What the evidence now supports differs from both original arguments. Proximity rather than size predicts use, and use is what produces benefit; a small park within a few minutes' walk is worth more than a large one across a main road. Quality of provision — seating, shade, toilets, lighting — determines who can use a space and for how long, and these are precisely the elements maintenance budgets cut first. The park's value is real, measurable and dependent on the least glamorous parts of its upkeep.

passages.title: Teaching the Body
passages.text:
A vaccine works by presenting the immune system with something recognisably foreign, without the disease that would normally accompany it. The system responds as it would to an infection — producing antibodies, and generating cells that persist — so that a later encounter with the real organism meets a response already prepared rather than one being assembled from scratch. The principle is simple and the difficulties lie entirely in the details.

The immune response has two components that are frequently conflated. Antibodies circulate and can neutralise a pathogen before it establishes itself, and their concentration falls over time, which is why antibody levels alone are a poor measure of protection. Memory cells persist and can regenerate a response quickly on re-exposure, and their persistence is often much longer than the antibodies. A person with low antibody levels may still be well protected, and a measurement showing decline is therefore not evidence that protection has gone.

What makes some diseases easy to vaccinate against and others hard is a property of the organism rather than of the science. A pathogen that changes little between generations presents a stable target, and a vaccine can remain effective for decades. One that mutates rapidly in the regions the immune system recognises presents a moving target requiring reformulation. Some organisms establish themselves in tissue the immune system reaches poorly, and some actively interfere with immune signalling, which is why decades of effort against certain diseases have produced partial results at best.

Population effects are where individual and collective interest diverge in a way worth stating plainly. Above a threshold of immunity in a population, transmission chains break and the organism cannot sustain itself, which protects those who are unvaccinated for medical reasons. The threshold depends on how transmissible the organism is and is high for the most transmissible ones. Below it, outbreaks resume, and the first cases are typically among those who could not be vaccinated rather than those who chose not to be.

The historical difficulty in demonstrating benefit is instructive and persists. A successful vaccination programme removes the disease from experience, so the risks it prevents become abstract while the risks of the vaccine — smaller, real and occurring in visible individuals — remain concrete. This asymmetry is structural. It intensifies as a programme succeeds, and it means public confidence tends to be lowest at the point of greatest success, when the least evidence of the original disease is available to anyone's memory.

The response supported by evidence is unglamorous. Correcting false claims performs poorly; making vaccination easy, default and convenient performs well. Most people who are not vaccinated in high-income settings are not refusing but have encountered friction — appointment systems, transport, working hours — and interventions that remove friction outperform those that address belief by a considerable margin.

passages.title: The Bargain of the Patent
passages.text:
A patent is a bargain rather than a right. In exchange for publishing how an invention works, the inventor receives a period during which others may not commercialise it. The intended effect is twofold: an incentive to invest in developing something copyable, and a body of disclosed technical knowledge that would otherwise be kept secret. Whether the bargain delivers either is an empirical question with an uncomfortable answer, which is that it depends enormously on the industry.

In pharmaceuticals the case is strongest. Development costs are large, the resulting product is cheap to copy once its composition is known, and without a period of exclusivity the investment would be difficult to justify. Studies of managers' own reports consistently find pharmaceuticals and chemicals at the top of any ranking of industries where patents are considered essential to appropriating returns.

In most other sectors the case is considerably weaker. Manufacturers surveyed repeatedly report that lead time, complementary manufacturing capability and secrecy protect innovations better than patents do, and that patents are sought mainly for defensive purposes — to avoid being sued, to trade in negotiations, or to signal capability to investors. Where firms accumulate patents primarily as bargaining assets, the disclosure function operates but the incentive function is doing little of the work its justification assumes.

Software has produced the clearest difficulties. Products combine thousands of separately patentable components, ownership is dispersed and difficult to establish in advance, and the boundaries of a claim are frequently unclear until litigated. This has enabled entities that produce nothing to acquire patents and extract settlements from firms that do, an activity whose legality is not in question and whose contribution to innovation is difficult to identify. Reforms have narrowed this and not closed it.

Alternatives exist and each solves part of the problem. Prizes reward a result without granting exclusivity, which suits well-defined targets and suits open-ended research poorly. Public funding produces knowledge without restriction and is weak at the expensive final stages of development. Advance purchase commitments guarantee a market for something not yet made and require the specification to be written before the solution is known. None dominates; each fits a different shape of problem.

What the evidence does not support is either general position in the public argument. Patents are not a universal engine of innovation, and abolishing them would not release a flood of suppressed invention. They function well in a small number of industries with a particular cost structure, poorly in several others, and the sensible design question is not whether to have them but whether a single instrument should apply uniformly across sectors whose economics have almost nothing in common.
